content: Endotracheal suctioning is a routine procedure performed on mechanically ventilated newborns in neonatal intensive care units. However, this procedure is associated with significant risks, including lobar collapse, pneumothorax, bradycardia, and hypoxemia. To mitigate these risks, the practice of increasing the inspired oxygen concentration immediately before suctioning, known as preoxygenation, has been proposed. The objective of this study was to evaluate the effects of preoxygenation compared to no preoxygenation during endotracheal suctioning in ventilated newborns. Additionally, subgroup analyses were planned to assess outcomes based on gestational age, the presence or absence of chronic lung disease, and the specific techniques used for endotracheal suctioning. A systematic search of databases, including MEDLINE (via PubMed), CINAHL, EMBASE, and The Cochrane Library, was conducted for studies published from 2007 to January 31, 2009. The search terms included oxygen, suction, preoxygenation, and pre-oxygenation, with limits applied to human studies, newborn infants, and clinical trials. No language restrictions were imposed. The inclusion criteria were randomized or quasi-randomized controlled trials involving mechanically ventilated neonates, comparing endotracheal suctioning with preoxygenation to suctioning without preoxygenation. Data collection and analysis followed the standard methods of the Cochrane Collaboration and the Neonatal Review Group. Trial quality was independently assessed, and data were extracted by the authors. Outcomes were analyzed using relative risk (RR) and risk difference (RD) for categorical data, and mean difference (MD) for continuous data, all with 95% confidence intervals. The review included one cross-over trial (Walsh 1987) involving 16 preterm neonates. Preoxygenation prior to endotracheal suctioning significantly reduced the incidence of hypoxemia (defined as transcutaneous partial pressure of oxygen [TcPO2] <40 mmHg). Specifically, the risk of hypoxemia was reduced at the end of the first suction (RR 0.18, 95% CI 0.05 to 0.69), at the end of the second suction (RR 0.23, 95% CI 0.08 to 0.66), and at 120 seconds after the second suction (RR 0.10, 95% CI 0.01 to 0.69). The mean TcPO2 was significantly higher in the preoxygenation group compared to the no preoxygenation group at the end of the first suction (MD 25.00 mmHg, 95% CI 14.20 to 35.80), at the end of the second suction (MD 24.80 mmHg, 95% CI 14.80 to 34.80), and at 120 seconds after the second suction (MD 29.10 mmHg, 95% CI 14.96 to 43.24). Additionally, the time required to return to baseline oxygenation levels was shorter in the preoxygenation group (MD -2.12 minutes, 95% CI -3.82 to -0.42). The authors concluded that the evidence from this review is insufficient to establish clinical practice guidelines. While preoxygenation was shown to reduce hypoxemia during suctioning, the findings are based on a single small trial of poor quality. Furthermore, other clinically important outcomes were not assessed. Additional high-quality studies are necessary to provide more robust evidence.
